fibonacci-number.pattern: From recursion to DP: memoise overlapping subproblems, then keep only the last two values

approaches.name: Plain recursion
approaches.idea: Write the definition directly: `F(n) = F(n − 1) + F(n − 2)`, with `F(0) = 0` and `F(1) = 1`.
approaches.why: Each call makes two more, and the same values are recomputed over and over (F(30) makes about 2.7 million calls). The recursion is n deep.

approaches.name: Memoisation (top-down DP)
approaches.idea: Same recursion, but store each `F(k)` the first time it is computed and reuse it afterwards. Every value is then computed once.
steps: `f(k)`: if `k < 2`, return `k`; if `memo[k]` is set, return it.
Otherwise compute `f(k − 1) + f(k − 2)`, store it in `memo[k]`, and return it.
approaches.why: Each of the n + 1 values is computed once in O(1). The memo table and the recursion stack are O(n).

approaches.name: Tabulation (bottom-up DP)
approaches.idea: Fill a table from the smallest values up, so each entry's two ingredients are ready when it is computed. No recursion.
steps: For `i` from 2 to n: `dp[i] = dp[i − 1] + dp[i − 2]`. Return `dp[n]`.
approaches.why: One loop of n steps and a table of n + 1 values.

approaches.name: Two variables
approaches.idea: Each value only needs the previous two, so keep just those two and slide them forward.
steps: Repeat n times: `(a, b) = (b, a + b)`.
approaches.why: n constant-time steps and two variables. (Matrix exponentiation can reach O(log n), which only pays off for huge n with modular arithmetic.)

climbing-stairs.pattern: 1-D DP: ways(i) = ways(i − 1) + ways(i − 2) (the last move was 1 or 2 steps)

approaches.name: Plain recursion over the last move
approaches.idea: To stand on step `n`, the last move came from step `n − 1` or `n − 2`. So the number of ways is the sum of the ways to reach those two steps.
steps: `ways(n)`: if `n <= 2`, return `n` (1 way for one step, 2 for two).
approaches.why: The call tree doubles at every level with massive repetition: n = 45 needs billions of calls.

approaches.name: Memoisation
approaches.idea: Cache `ways(k)` so each step count is solved only once.
steps: `ways(k)`: return `k` if `k <= 2`; return the cached value if there is one.
Otherwise compute `ways(k − 1) + ways(k − 2)`, cache it, and return it.
approaches.why: n distinct subproblems, O(1) each; the cache and the call stack hold O(n).

approaches.name: Tabulation
approaches.idea: Fill `dp[i]` = ways to reach step `i`, from the bottom up.
steps: For `i` from 3 to n: `dp[i] = dp[i − 1] + dp[i − 2]`.

approaches.name: Two variables
approaches.idea: Only the ways for the previous two steps are ever needed, so keep two numbers instead of a table.
steps: Repeat n − 1 times: `(a, b) = (b, a + b)` — each repeat moves both one step up.
Return `a`, which is now the number of ways to reach step n.
approaches.why: n steps with two variables. The answer for n = 45 is 1,836,311,903, just under 2³¹, so a 32-bit int is enough.

min-cost-climbing-stairs.pattern: 1-D DP: cheapest cost to stand at step i = cost[i] + min of the two steps before

approaches.name: Recursion over the last jump
approaches.idea: Let `reach(i)` be the cheapest cost to arrive at position `i` (before paying for it). You arrive from `i − 1` or `i − 2`, paying for that stair. Positions 0 and 1 cost nothing to reach.
approaches.why: Two recursive calls per position with heavy repetition; only usable for tiny inputs.

approaches.name: Memoisation
approaches.idea: Same recurrence, caching `reach(i)` so each position is solved once.
steps: `reach(i)`: return 0 for `i <= 1`; return the cached value if present.
Otherwise compute the minimum of the two options, cache it, and return it.
approaches.why: n + 1 subproblems at O(1) each; the cache and the recursion stack are O(n).

approaches.name: Tabulation
approaches.idea: Fill `dp[i]` = cheapest cost to reach position `i`, for `i` from 2 up to n (the top).
steps: For `i` from 2 to n: `dp[i] = min(dp[i − 1] + cost[i − 1], dp[i − 2] + cost[i − 2])`.

approaches.name: Two rolling values
approaches.idea: `dp[i]` depends only on `dp[i − 1]` and `dp[i − 2]`, so two variables replace the table.
steps: Set `a = 0` (position i − 2) and `b = 0` (position i − 1), starting at i = 2.
For `i` from 2 to n: `next = min(b + cost[i − 1], a + cost[i − 2])`; then `a = b`, `b = next`.

n-th-tribonacci-number.pattern: 1-D DP over the last three values

approaches.name: Plain recursion
approaches.idea: Follow the definition: `T(n) = T(n − 1) + T(n − 2) + T(n − 3)`, with `T(0) = 0`, `T(1) = T(2) = 1`.
approaches.why: Three calls per level with heavy repetition — the call count itself grows like the sequence (about 1.84ⁿ), billions for n = 37.

approaches.name: Memoisation
approaches.idea: Cache each `T(k)` the first time it is computed.
steps: `t(k)`: base cases as before; return the cached value if present.
Otherwise compute the sum of the three previous terms, cache it, return it.
approaches.why: n + 1 subproblems with O(1) work each; the cache and recursion take O(n).

approaches.name: Three rolling variables
approaches.idea: Each term needs only the previous three, so slide a window of three values forward.
steps: Repeat n times: `(a, b, c) = (b, c, a + b + c)` — the window moves one term forward.
approaches.why: n constant-time steps and three variables. T(37) = 2,082,876,103 fits in a 32-bit int, but the values computed ahead of it do not, so Java and C++ use 64-bit variables.
